papers.title: LTPat-based SOXFE: A self-organized explainable feature engineering model for automated fibromyalgia detection.
papers.abstract: BackgroundFibromyalgia is a chronic pain disorder associated with sleep disturbance and substantial functional burden.ObjectiveThis study evaluated a self-organized explainable feature engineering (SOXFE) model for EEG-based fibromyalgia classification.MethodsA previously reported sleep EEG dataset from a 32-participant source cohort was analyzed separately for NREM Stage 2 and Stage 3. The analysis-ready version contained 136 labeled stage-record files: 74 for Stage 2 and 62 for Stage 3. The SOXFE model comprised LTPat feature extraction, training-only CWNCA feature selection, tkNN classification, IMV information fusion, and DLob-based explanation. Record-wise LORO was primary; segment-level 10-fold cross-validation was complementary.ResultsRecord-wise LORO used 74 outer folds for Stage 2 and 62 for Stage 3. Descriptive pooled held-out-epoch accuracy was 92.77% (95% CI: 91.76-93.67) for Stage 2 and 97.00% (95% CI: 96.22-97.63) for Stage 3. Every epoch from the held-out recording was excluded from training and selection. Complementary segment-level 10-fold cross-validation yielded 100.00% accuracy for both stages but was not used as evidence of record-wise generalization.ConclusionsThe model provided record-disjoint classification and traceable model-derived explanations in this single-source dataset. LORO prevented within-record epoch leakage. However, participant linkage was unavailable, so records from the same person may have occurred across outer partitions and the reported values may overestimate person-independent performance. Verified subject-wise validation is required before clinical use.

papers.title: Complementing Engel Classification: Postoperative Scalp EEG as an Objective Indicator in SEEG-Guided Radiofrequency Thermocoagulation-A Seizure-Onset Pattern-Based Stratified Analysis.
papers.abstract: Stereoelectroencephalography-guided radiofrequency thermocoagulation (SEEG-RFTC) is a minimally invasive therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. However, the relationship between specific seizure-onset patterns (SOPs), particularly low-voltage fast activity (LVFA), and postoperative scalp EEG normalization remains inadequately characterized. This study investigates whether LVFA predicts RFTC efficacy and whether postoperative EEG serves as an objective complement to clinical outcome measures. To evaluate LVFA-dominant SOPs as predictors of seizure freedom and scalp EEG normalization after SEEG-RFTC, and to assess their interaction with MRI findings. In a retrospective cohort of 25 patients, seizure-onset patterns (SOPs) were classified as LVFA-present (n = 13) or LVFA-absent (n = 12). Outcomes included Engel classification and 6-month postoperative scalp EEG. Seizure freedom and EEG normalization rates were compared, with MRI-stratified analysis. The seizure-free rate was 92.3% (12/13) in the LVFA-present group versus 33.3% (4/12) in the LVFA-absent group (p = 0.004). EEG normalization was more frequent in LVFA-present patients (7/8, 87.5%) than in LVFA-absent patients (4/12, 33.3%; p = 0.028); all but one patient with EEG normalization was seizure-free, the sole exception being an LVFA-absent patient who remained Engel III. In MRI-negative patients, LVFA-present had 100% (6/6) seizure freedom versus 20.0% (1/5) without LVFA (p = 0.015). Scalp EEG normalization may serve as a relatively objective marker of complete disintegration of the epileptic network, whereas some patients with persistent EEG abnormalities may still achieve seizure freedom with the aid of antiseizure medications. In this cohort, LVFA-present SOPs are strongly associated with favorable RFTC outcomes and may represent a prerequisite for postoperative scalp EEG normalization. Postoperative EEG is a sensitive objective endpoint that complements Engel classification. Systematic PET evaluation in larger cohorts may further refine candidate selection in MRI-negative patients.

papers.title: Efficacy and acceptability of digital safety planning therapy for self-injurious thoughts and behaviors in adolescents with depressive episodes: a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Self-injurious thoughts and behaviors (SITB) represent a significant mental health issue among Chinese adolescents. Research on smartphone-based safety planning as digital therapeutics for SITB in China remains limited. This randomized controlled trial evaluated the efficacy and acceptability of a safety planning mobile application (LIFES) for reducing SITB in adolescents with depressive episodes. Among 189 adolescents with depressive episodes screened, 122 were randomized to either the intervention group (LIFES app plus treatment as usual [TAU], n = 61) or the control group (TAU only, n = 61). Follow-up assessments at 1, 3, and 6 months measured SITB, depression, anxiety, and sleep quality. This trial is registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2300075663; https://www.chictr.org.cn/). Generalized linear mixed models showed significant time-by-group interaction effects for non-suicidal self-injury frequency (F = 3.39, p = .018), suicide planning seriousness (F = 2.93, p = .034), confidence in suicide completion during preparation (F = 3.10, p = .027), suicide threat/gesture frequency (F = 3.64, p = .013), and total suicidal behavior frequency (F = 3.31, p = .020) after adjusting for depression and anxiety symptom severity, sleep quality, and years of education. The intervention group showed significantly greater reductions in SITB characteristics compared to the control group. User experience surveys indicated good satisfaction with the application. This study demonstrates that safety planning-based digital therapeutics are an effective adjunctive intervention for SITB in adolescents with depressive episodes. Future research should examine the applicability of this intervention to broader populations.

papers.title: Endotypic Traits of Hypopnea-Predominant OSA: The Role of Hypopnea Criteria.
papers.abstract: Hypopnea-predominant OSA (HypoOSA) represents a distinct phenotype compared to apnea-predominant OSA. Nevertheless, hypopnea has been defined using varying criteria, leading to differences in the estimation of AHI. This study investigated the endotypic traits of HypoOSA, as defined by ≥ 4% desaturation (4% OD) and ≥ 3% desaturation or arousal (3% ODA) criteria for hypopnea and how AHI and endotypic traits differ by criteria. We prospectively enrolled 765 adult patients with moderate-to-severe OSA from a single sleep centre. Endotypic traits were obtained from in-laboratory polysomnographic studies. Respiratory events were scored twice using 3% ODA and 4% OD criteria. Endotypic traits characterizing HypoOSA, defined as AHI comprising < 50% apneas, were identified and compared to apnea-predominant OSA. Within-subject differences in endotypic traits between the hypopnea criteria were analysed. We observed that 4% OD and 3% ODA identified 40.3% and 57.0% patients as HypoOSA, respectively. Compared to apnea-predominant OSA, HypoOSA was characterized by a lower arousal threshold, higher compensation and less collapsible upper airway, regardless of hypopnea criteria used. Compared with the 4% OD criterion, the 3% ODA criterion for hypopnea increased AHI by 33%, whereas the proportion of time with SpO2 < 90% and endotypic traits showed less variation. Patients with low consistency in AHI estimates between the two criteria showed lower AHI and favourable upper airway pathology compared to the high consistency group. In conclusion, HypoOSA is characterized by lower arousal threshold and favourable upper airway patency. Different hypopnea criteria resulted in variation in AHI, particularly among patients with lower AHI, whereas hypoxic burden and endotypic traits remained relatively stable.

papers.title: When Mothers are About to Return to Work After Maternity Leave: A Descriptive Study in the Netherlands.
papers.abstract: The return to work after maternity leave is reported to be a stressful event for many mothers. Yet, little is known about their experience just before returning. This descriptive study explored mothers' evaluation of this period, their levels of anticipatory postpartum work resumption stress (APWRS), their caregiving decisions, and factors that could support them. Self-reported data were collected from 236 Dutch mothers of infants planning to return to work within the next month. One in five mothers in our sample assigned an unsatisfactory evaluation rating (five or below) to the period before the return. While mothers reported experiencing concerns about work-family imbalance and child separation, many mothers also expressed positive thoughts and emotions about their upcoming return. Two-thirds made adjustments to infant care in preparation for their return to work, such as adjusting infant sleep routines, starting with bottle feeding, and weaning off or stopping breastfeeding. Mothers who made caregiving changes experienced greater APWRS. Social support, longer leave, gradual work re-entry, better sleep, and improved health were identified to benefit mothers approaching the transition to postpartum employment. Additionally, mothers experiencing higher levels of both near-environment and workplace support reported lower levels of APWRS and assigned a higher evaluation rating to the period before returning to work. Our findings highlight the need for further research on the period prior to mothers' return to work, specifically regarding how they feel, the caregiving practices they consequently adopt, and how they can be supported.

papers.title: When Charon Knocks at the Sleep Laboratory: Are European Heatwaves an Underrecognized Methodological Challenge for Sleep Research?

Cannabis for sleep in older adults: use has outpaced the science.
papers.abstract: Cannabis use among older adults, defined here as those over 50 years of age, has increased rapidly, and sleep disturbance is among the most common reasons for use. Yet, despite growing use of cannabis and individual cannabinoids to facilitate sleep, evidence supporting their efficacy, tolerability and safety in older adults remains limited. Most experimental studies of cannabinoids and sleep have been conducted in younger adults, often using products and formulations that differ substantially from those currently available. The subjective perception of improved sleep, which may drive increased use is often not supported by objective polysomnography or actigraphy data. Aging is accompanied by changes in sleep physiology, pharmacokinetics, body composition, the endocannabinoid system, multimorbidity, and polypharmacy that may alter cannabinoid effects. As a result, findings derived from younger populations may not generalize to older adults. Furthermore, regular and repeated use of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabis leads to the development of tolerance and withdrawal-related sleep disruption complicates interpretation of longer-term effects. The evidence for cannabidiol (CBD) and cannabinol (CBN) in sleep remains sparse. Rigorous studies specifically enrolling older adults are virtually nonexistent. Given the rapid growth of cannabis use for sleep in this population, randomized controlled trials incorporating both subjective and objective sleep measures, age-specific pharmacokinetics, drug interactions, and longer-term outcomes are urgently needed to guide clinical care.

papers.title: Advantage of cerebellar intermittent theta-burst stimulation in Alzheimer's disease (ACT-AD): study protocol for a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial.
papers.abstract: The cerebellum plays a crucial role in cognitive processing and thus presents a promising therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease (AD). This trial aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of long-term, neuronavigated cerebellar intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) in patients with AD. The ACT-AD trial is a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled study involving 100 participants with mild-to-moderate AD across 4 centers in China. Participants will be randomized to receive either cerebellar iTBS or sham stimulation for 4 weeks (daily sessions), followed by 8 weeks of weekly maintenance sessions. The primary outcome is the change in the Clinical Dementia Rating Scale Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) score from baseline to week 12. Secondary outcomes include additional clinical scales. Exploratory outcomes include electroencephalogram (EEG), blood biomarkers and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Statistical analysis will follow intention-to-treat principles using mixed models for repeated measures (MMRM). The ACT-AD trial will assess the efficacy and safety of long-term, neuronavigated cerebellar iTBS in treating patients with mild-to-moderate AD. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06669182. Registered on 31 October 2024.

papers.title: How auditory rhythm perception shapes speech production: The influence of neural synchronization and rhythmic patterns.
papers.abstract: Auditory rhythm perception facilitates language processing, yet it remains unclear how neural synchronization to external rhythms contributes to speech production. The present study examined whether individual differences in neural synchronization modulate rhythmic priming effects during speech production and whether such effects depend on the rhythmic structure of the target utterance. Eighty-six native Mandarin speakers performed a speech production task involving two four-syllable rhythmic patterns as targets: the dominant [2+2] pattern (boundary after the second syllable) and the less common [1+3] pattern (boundary after the first syllable). Each target was preceded by a rhythmically congruent or incongruent pure-tone prime. Neural synchronization to the primes was quantified using cerebral-acoustic coherence (CACoh) between EEG activity and the temporal envelope of the auditory rhythms, and rhythmic priming was assessed using response latencies. K-means clustering of CACoh measures identified two participant groups characterized by relatively high and low levels of neural synchronization. Behavioral analyses revealed a significant Group × Target Type interaction. For the less common [1+3] pattern, low synchronizers exhibited reliable rhythmic priming, whereas high synchronizers showed little or no priming benefit. In contrast, priming effects for the dominant [2+2] pattern were modest and comparable across groups. Furthermore, higher theta-band CACoh was associated with smaller priming effects for [1+3] targets, indicating that stronger neural synchronization predicted reduced behavioral facilitation. These findings suggest that the influence of auditory rhythm on speech production depends jointly on individual neural synchronization capacity and the rhythmic structure of the planned utterance. The results provide new evidence that auditory-motor interactions in speech production are shaped by both listener-specific and utterance-specific factors.

papers.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea severity and insulin resistance in children with Prader-Willi Syndrome: the SPISE index as a candidate metabolic marker.
papers.abstract: We compared two surrogate markers of insulin sensitivity - the single-point insulin sensitivity estimator (SPISE) and HOMA-IR - and evaluated their associations with OSA severity in children with genetically confirmed PWS and a symptomatic non-syndromic referral group (NSR) with available polysomnography (PSG) and fasting biochemical data. In this single-centre retrospective cross-sectional study, OSA severity was indexed by the obstructive apnoea-hypopnoea index (oAHI), central AHI (cAHI) and oxygen desaturation index (ODI), and caregiver-reported symptoms by the PSQ-SRBD scale. Multivariable models were fitted within the PWS group. Of 458 PSG studies screened, 31 children with PWS and 47 NSR met the inclusion criteria. cAHI was higher in PWS (p < 0.001), and PSQ-SRBD scores were slightly lower, despite a similar oAHI distribution. Within the PWS group, oAHI correlated inversely with SPISE (ρ = - 0.378, p = 0.036). In multivariable models adjusted for age, sex, BMI-SDS, and growth hormone therapy, higher oAHI was associated with lower SPISE (B = - 0.154, p = 0.015), whereas the association with ln(HOMA-IR) was borderline (B = 0.081, p = 0.0497). ODI correlated with SPISE (ρ = - 0.427, p = 0.017) but not with HOMA-IR (ρ = 0.319, p = 0.081). Phase-stratified analyses showed oAHI-SPISE correlations in phases 2 and 3 and an oAHI-HOMA-IR correlation in phase 3. In children with PWS, OSA severity was associated with markers of impaired insulin sensitivity. The associations of SPISE with oAHI and ODI support its further investigation as a candidate metabolic correlate of OSA severity. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger independent cohorts. • OSA is highly prevalent in PWS. OSA severity is associated with insulin resistance in adults and in non-syndromic children with obesity, but this relationship and the insulin-independent SPISE index have not been evaluated in PWS. • OSA severity was associated with impaired insulin sensitivity markers in children with PWS. • SPISE, derived from lipids and BMI without fasting insulin, was associated with oAHI and ODI in PWS; it merits further investigation as a candidate metabolic correlate of OSA severity.

A Prospective, Observational, Open-Label, Nonrandomized, Multicenter Study Measuring Functional Outcomes in a Novel Interspinous Stabilization Device in Patients With Low Back Pain: 12-Month Results for the REFINE Study.
papers.abstract: Lumbar spinal stenosis associated with degenerative disc disease is a common source of pain and reduced quality of life in older adults. Current focus has centered on minimally invasive options. Previous reports of the performance of a novel standalone interlaminar fixation device have been previously reported. This cohort represents the 12-month outcomes, looking at safety and efficacy. Ninety-four patients underwent implantation, and 79 completed follow-ups. The primary endpoint was a composite clinical success, incorporating the absence of index-level revision or reoperation, clinically meaningful improvement in pain using the visual analog scale, disability improvement as measured by the Oswestry Disability Index, and better disease-specific status as measured by the Zurich Claudication Questionnaire. Secondary outcomes included changes in PROMIS-29 and Patient Global Impression of Change. Safety assessment included adverse events, readmissions, and reoperations. Analyses used the implanted cohort with paired comparisons for follow-up data and interpretation using prespecified minimal clinically important difference thresholds. Patients demonstrated statistically significant improvement in disability, pain, and disease-specific function. Mean Oswestry Disability Index improved by 22.0 points; back and leg pain visual analog scale score improved by 35.7 and 36.5 points, respectively. Zurich Claudication Questionnaire symptom severity and physical function also improved, and PROMIS-29 domains were favorable across pain interference, sleep disturbance, fatigue, anxiety, depression, social roles, and physicality. Patient Global Impression of Change responses indicated 83% of patients reported at least minimal improvement. Six adverse events were reported, 3 of which were deemed related to the device or procedure. No index-level reoperations, device explants, or symptomatic spinous process fractures were reported. In this prospective multicenter cohort, standalone interlaminar fixation produced clinically meaningful improvement in pain, disability, and patient-reported quality of life. This study represents the first prospectively acquired data for a posterior interspinous fixation device used without other instrumentation to treat systematic spinal stenosis in the presence of degenerative disc disease. Level 2: prospective, nonrandomized, multicenter trial.

papers.title: Bedtime technology activities and multidimensional sleep health in rural Appalachian adults: Findings from the REST-KY study.
papers.abstract: Bedtime technology use is frequently associated with poor sleep outcomes, yet evidence examining the impacts of specific technologies on multidimensional sleep health remains limited, particularly in health disparity populations. We examined associations between bedtime technology activities and sleep health in rural Appalachian adults. The sample comprised 375 adults from 12 economically distressed counties in Eastern Kentucky. Participants completed online surveys assessing bedtime technology use in the hour before sleep and sleep health across 8 dimensions (satisfaction, alertness, timing, efficiency, duration, duration irregularity, social jetlag, and wake after sleep onset), operationalized as an extended sleep health score (range: 0-8). Linear regression models examined associations between technology use frequency (frequent vs. infrequent) and overall sleep health, adjusting for sociodemographic factors, mental health symptoms, chronotype, and sleep medication use. Logistic regression explored dimension-specific associations for various technology types. Most participants (73.3%) were female and White (97.3%) (mAge 45.6 [range 18-81: SD = 13.1]); mean extended sleep health score was 5.1 (SD = 1.7). In adjusted models, less frequent work-related computer use was associated with higher extended sleep health scores (mean difference = 0.70, 95% CI: 0.26-1.14). Dimension-specific analyses linked infrequent work-related computer use to favorable alertness (OR = 2.33, 95% CI: 1.21-4.49) and wake after sleep onset (OR = 3.15, 95% CI: 1.41-6.98). Differential associations across technology types and sleep dimensions suggest that cognitively engaging, work-related technology use (e.g., work-related computer use) may be particularly detrimental to sleep, highlighting the importance of examining specific technology use patterns in sleep health interventions for rural, health disparate populations.

papers.title: Rest-activity rhythms, sleep dimensions, and mortality in adults with cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome: A survey-weighted NHANES cohort study.
papers.abstract: To examine rest-activity rhythms and objective sleep dimensions with all-cause mortality, with heart-disease mortality as a supportive secondary outcome, among adults with cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome. We analyzed National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2011-2014 data linked to mortality through 2019 among adults with archived cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic stages 1 to 4. Rest-activity rhythm metrics (interdaily stability, intradaily variability, relative amplitude) and sleep parameters (duration, efficiency, timing variability) were derived from wrist-worn actigraphy. Survey-weighted Cox models incorporated mobile examination center weights, strata, and primary sampling units. Among 3061 participants, 274 all-cause and 79 heart-disease deaths occurred. Higher intradaily variability was associated with higher all-cause mortality (hazard ratio [HR] per 0.1 unit, 1.15; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.08-1.23), whereas higher relative amplitude was associated with lower mortality (HR per 0.1 unit, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.66-0.82). Longer mean sleep duration (HR per hour, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.74-0.91) and higher sleep efficiency (HR per 0.1-unit increase, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.57-0.86) were associated with lower all-cause mortality, whereas greater sleep-midpoint variability was associated with higher all-cause mortality (HR per hour, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.04-1.52). Associations of relative amplitude and mean sleep duration with all-cause mortality were nonlinear. Heart-disease mortality findings were supportive. Greater rest-activity rhythm fragmentation, lower rest-activity rhythm amplitude, and several sleep dimensions were associated with all-cause mortality. These findings do not establish causality or clinical thresholds.

papers.title: Comparison of rest-activity rhythm metrics derived from Oura ring and actiwatch devices: A device validation and analytical pipeline comparison study.
papers.abstract: Non-parametric rest-activity rhythm (RAR) metrics are increasingly used as 24-hour behavioral markers of circadian and general health. Although traditionally derived from research-grade actigraphy, consumer wearables may provide scalable alternatives for long-term monitoring. This study evaluated the performance of RAR metrics derived from Oura Ring versus Actiwatch (AW2) during concurrent wear and examined the influence of analytic pipeline. Forty-one healthy adults (mean age 26.3 years; 27 female) wore both devices for 14 days. Interdaily stability (IS), intradaily variability (IV), relative amplitude (RA), and L5/M10 timing were calculated using nparACT, MotionWare, and a custom pipeline. Performance was evaluated using ICC(A,1), ICC(C,1), Spearman's ρ, and Bland-Altman analysis. Oura MET was zero-referenced from its resting floor of 0.9 for RA analysis. Participants contributed a mean of 10.6 valid concurrent wear days. Oura Ring had slightly higher IS and lower IV than AW2. IS, IV, L5/M10 timing, and RA all showed moderate-to-excellent absolute agreement (ICC[A,1] = 0.67-0.98) and strong rank-order associations (Spearman's ρ = 0.71-0.98). Estimates were similar across the 3 analytical pipelines, although differences in M10/L5 implementation influenced timing estimates in one outlier. Oura-derived RAR metrics showed acceptable overall agreement with AW2 when the known difference in measurement origin was accounted for in the RA calculation. Results were generally consistent across analytic pipelines, supporting analytic reproducibility. The M10 outlier showed that unusual activity values on individual days can affect M10 estimates across pipelines.

papers.title: Revisiting post-stimulus theta activity: evidence for a broadband rather than narrowband spectral origin.
papers.abstract: The aperiodic, 1/f-like component of electrophysiological activity is increasingly recognized as a meaningful feature of neural function rather than background noise. Meanwhile, many EEG studies interpret transient post-stimulus changes in oscillatory power as signatures of attention, salience, or cognitive control. Such interpretations typically depend on baseline normalization, which assumes aperiodic activity remains stable from pre- to post-stimulus periods. Using high-density EEG from typically developing children, we tested this assumption across two paradigms: an audiovisual simple reaction-time task (n = 36, 19 males and 17 females) and a visual oddball task (n = 38, 20 males and 18 females). In each, conventional spectral analyses were compared with analyses that explicitly modeled and removed aperiodic activity in both windows. Across tasks, stimulus onset produced robust increases in aperiodic exponent and offset, indicating systematic 1/f changes. In the audiovisual task these were modality-specific, with central, parieto-occipital, or combined topographies by stimulus type. They diminished but persisted after ERP removal, suggesting they were not fully explained by phase-locked activity. Critically, once aperiodic activity was accounted for, the apparent theta increase was largely abolished in both tasks, including the canonical fronto-central enhancement to infrequent targets. The conventional method also overestimated beta desynchronization, especially in the induced signal, indicating a spurious consequence of spectral slope steepening. By contrast, alpha desynchronization remained robust and was enhanced, reflecting genuine suppression. Together, these findings suggest many conventional time-frequency effects, particularly apparent theta synchronization, may reflect stimulus-driven aperiodic changes rather than robust narrowband changes, challenging core assumptions of these analyses.Significance statement Frequency-domain neural activity comprises both narrowband oscillations and broadband aperiodic activity. Conventional time-frequency analyses use baseline normalization to isolate oscillatory responses, implicitly assuming that aperiodic activity remains stable following stimulus onset. Across two EEG paradigms, we show that stimulus presentation systematically alters aperiodic activity in a sensory- and attention-dependent manner. These changes can produce apparent increases in theta-band power that do not reflect genuine narrowband oscillations and can exaggerate beta desynchronization. In contrast, alpha desynchronization remained robust after accounting for aperiodic activity. These findings demonstrate that stimulus-related aperiodic changes can substantially influence conventional time-frequency measures and should be explicitly considered when interpreting post-stimulus oscillatory responses.

papers.title: A Randomized Clinical Trial of Transcutaneous Electrical Acupoint Stimulation for Pain Relief After Dental Implant Surgery.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the clinical efficacy of transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation (TEAS) on postoperative pain, sleep quality, and swelling following dental implant surgery. A randomized, sham-controlled, double-blind clinical trial was conducted. A total of 64 patients who underwent single-tooth implant surgery without bone grafting at the Chongqing Medical University Affiliated Stomatological Hospital between June 2024 and June 2026 were enrolled and randomly assigned to either the TEAS group (n = 32) or the Mock group (n = 32). In the TEAS group, stimulation was applied at the Hegu (LI4) and Laogong (PC8) acupoints for 30 min using a 2/100 Hz variable-frequency current, once 30 min before surgery and again 30 min after surgery. The Mock group received electrode pads attached to the same acupoints without electrical output. The primary outcome was the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score on the night of surgery (POD 1) and on POD 2 and 3. Secondary outcomes included total sleep duration, sleep efficiency, and local swelling score. Baseline demographic characteristics did not differ significantly between the two groups (p > 0.05). On the night of surgery, the VAS pain score in the TEAS group was significantly lower than that in the Mock group (1.719 ± 1.397 vs. 3.094 ± 2.100, p = 0.003), but not on POD 2 or POD 3 (p > 0.05). Total sleep duration was significantly longer in the TEAS group than in the Mock group on both the night of surgery and POD 2 (p < 0.05), but not on POD 3 (p > 0.05). Sleep efficiency did not differ significantly between groups at any time point (p > 0.05). On POD 3, the swelling score in the TEAS group was significantly lower than that in the Mock group (0.813 ± 0.896 vs. 1.438 ± 1.045, p = 0.013), whereas no significant differences were found on the night of surgery or POD 2 (p > 0.05). TEAS may reduce early postoperative pain (within the first 24 h), prolong sleep duration on the night of surgery and POD 2, and reduce local swelling on POD 3 after dental implant surgery. These findings support the use of TEAS as an effective adjunctive modality within a multimodal analgesia protocol for dental implant surgery.

papers.title: Weight Management in Obesity-Associated Sleep-Disordered Breathing: Mechanisms, Clinical Management, and Emerging Therapies.
papers.abstract: To review the mechanistic links between obesity and sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) and summarize practical approaches to weight-directed, sleep-directed, and phenotype-informed management. We conducted a focused narrative review of clinical trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, guidelines, and mechanistic studies identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Google Scholar. Search terms included obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, obesity hypoventilation syndrome, weight loss, positive airway pressure, bariatric surgery, incretin-based pharmacotherapy, endotypes, and circadian disruption. Obesity promotes sleep-disordered breathing through upper airway mechanical loading, reduced lung volumes, inflammation, altered ventilatory control, and sleep behavior pathways. Positive airway pressure remains a core therapy for many patients with obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Sustained weight loss provides complementary disease modification. Lifestyle intervention, metabolic and bariatric surgery, and incretin based pharmacotherapy can improve obstructive sleep apnea, although residual disease is common. Tirzepatide has shown clinically meaningful reductions in apnea-hypopnea index in adults with obesity and moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea, largely in association with weight reduction. In obesity hypoventilation syndrome, stable ambulatory patients generally require positive airway pressure. Durable weight loss of approximately 25% to 30% may be needed to resolve hypoventilation. Therapies targeting endotypes and device based options may help selected patients, but they remain adjunctive, investigational, or directed by specialists. Obesity associated sleep-disordered breathing is best managed as a heterogeneous cardiometabolic and sleep breathing condition. Treatment should integrate positive airway pressure or other sleep specific therapy with individualized weight management. Ongoing reassessment is needed for residual disease, obesity hypoventilation syndrome, and atypical phenotypes.

papers.title: Hemoglobin Exhibits a U-Shaped Association with Obstructive Sleep Apnea at High Altitude: Machine-Learning and Exploratory Interventional Evidence.
papers.abstract: Chronic high-altitude hypoxia induces adaptive erythrocytosis, but the relationship between hemoglobin (Hb) and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) remains unclear. We examined the association between Hb levels and OSA severity and explored short-term changes in sleep-related outcomes after erythrocytapheresis. 250 men residing ≥1 year above 3,000 m were recruited at 3,860 m. OSA was assessed by portable polysomnography (apnea-hypopnea index, AHI; oxygenation). Participants were stratified by Hb level (<170, 170-210, and ≥210 g/L). Machine-learning classification and restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses were used to evaluate nonlinear Hb-OSA associations. In the substudy, 15 participants with Hb >240 g/L underwent erythrocytapheresis, and 15 contemporaneous participants with high-altitude polycythemia (HAPC) received oxygen therapy alone. Sleep was reassessed within 24-48 h. A U-shaped relationship between Hb and AHI was observed, with the lowest AHI in the 170-210 g/L group (P < 0.001). RCS analysis confirmed a significant nonlinear association (P < 0.001). The machine-learning model for OSA classification achieved an AUC of 0.873, with BMI, daytime SpO2, and Hb deviation contributing to risk stratification. In the exploratory substudy, erythrocytapheresis was associated with larger short-term reductions in Hb and AHI, and with improved nocturnal oxygenation, compared with oxygen therapy alone. Hb showed a nonlinear, U-shaped association with OSA at high altitude. Intermediate Hb levels (170-210 g/L) were associated with more favorable sleep-related indices. Erythrocytapheresis was associated with short-term improvement in sleep-related measures among participants with HAPC, supporting further controlled evaluation.

papers.title: Genome-wide association studies of osteoarthritis: from genetic discovery to precision medicine.
papers.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) affects more than 500 million people worldwide, yet disease-modifying therapies remain unavailable. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have transformed understanding of OA genetic susceptibility, progressing from early single-cohort analyses to multi-ancestry meta-analyses involving 2 million individuals and prioritizing hundreds of loci and 700 effector genes. This review summarizes the development of OA GWAS and examines how genetic discoveries are being translated into biological mechanisms and precision medicine. We discuss how integrating GWAS with fine-mapping, molecular quantitative trait loci (QTLs), chromatin interaction maps, single-cell and spatial omics, proteomics and metabolomics links non-coding signals to effector genes, regulatory programs and disease-relevant cell states. These genes converge on biological modules involving developmental patterning, extracellular matrix homeostasis, metabolism, immune-inflammatory signaling, circadian regulation and neuro-glial pathways, linking inherited susceptibility to joint structure, tissue homeostasis and symptoms. We further review translational applications, including Mendelian randomization, GWAS-informed drug target prioritization, polygenic risk scores for risk stratification and precision prevention, and AI-enabled multimodal models for phenotype refinement, subgrouping and trial enrichment. Finally, we highlight key challenges, including phenotype heterogeneity, ancestry imbalance, incomplete variant-to-function mapping and limited clinical validation. Addressing these challenges is essential for translating OA GWAS into globally relevant, mechanism-based and precision-oriented prevention and treatment.

papers.title: Structure-activity relationships of BnOCPA derivatives at native pre- and postsynaptic adenosine A1Rs.
papers.abstract: The addition of a benzyloxy group to the adenosine A1R agonist cyclopentyladenosine (CPA) produces a compound (BnOCPA) that selectivity activates A1R signalling via the G protein alpha subunit Gob. In rat hippocampus, BnOCPA inhibits CA3-CA1 synaptic transmission (IC50 65 nM) likely via Gob, with no effect on Goa-mediated postsynaptic membrane electrophysiology at concentrations up to 1 μM. We have investigated how modifications of the benzyloxy group of BnOCPA affects signalling: addition of methoxy group, MBnOCPA, substituting a phenoxy group, PhOCPA; and addition of bromide to the phenoxy group, BPhOCPA. These derivatives, previously shown to be selective A1R agonists, were assessed through inhibition of hippocampal CA3-CA1 synaptic transmission and postsynaptic effects on CA1 pyramidal neurons. All compounds inhibited synaptic transmission and increased paired-pulse facilitation, indicative of presynaptic actions. At a concentration that inhibited synaptic transmission (>75 %), none of the compounds hyperpolarised the resting membrane potential and thus retained the pre- vs postsynaptic selectivity of BnOCPA. Increasing their concentration allowed a measure of the selectivity range. BnOCPA hyperpolarised ∼ 40 % of neurons at 3 μM (∼ 50x the IC50 for synaptic inhibition). For PhOCPA and MBnOCPA, hyperpolarisation, occurred for some neurons, at 1 μM. For BPhOCPA, no hyperpolarisation occurred at concentrations up to 10 μM. Pre-application of the derivatives (at 300 nM) reduced adenosine-mediated hyperpolarisation, showing they bind but do not activate postsynaptic A1Rs. This data shows that modifying the structure of BnOCPA changes the discrimination between different native A1Rs, likely based upon selective activation of G-protein coupling.

papers.title: Distinct brain network organization in asynchronous and synchronous motor observation and motor imagery: evidence from EEG functional connectivity, phase-amplitude coupling, and decoding.
papers.abstract: Motor observation and motor imagery (MOMI) has been increasingly utilized in motor learning and neurorehabilitation research; however, it remains unclear whether different temporal arrangements of observation and imagery are reflected in distinct brain network organization. Therefore, the present study investigated whether asynchronous and synchronous MOMI exhibit distinct network-level patterns during motor simulation. To isolate the effect of temporal organization while maintaining a constant motor task context, participants performed a basketball set-shot task, allowing comparison among asynchronous MOMI (A-MOMI), synchronous MOMI (S-MOMI), and motor imagery (MI). Phase-locking value (PLV)-based functional connectivity analyses revealed significant condition-related differences, predominantly within the theta, alpha, and beta frequency bands. Specifically, MI exhibited stronger theta-band functional connectivity during the early phase of the task, whereas A-MOMI demonstrated more sustained enhancement of alpha-band connectivity during the middle and later phases. Furthermore, coupling between theta phase and 12-16 Hz amplitude was stronger in A-MOMI compared to both S-MOMI and MI. Decoding analysis further indicated moderate separability among the three conditions, yielding an overall classification accuracy of 69.61%. A-MOMI achieved the highest classification accuracy (79.41%), followed by MI (73.53%) and S-MOMI (55.88%), reflecting differential discriminability among the conditions. Collectively, these findings provide network-level evidence that the temporal organization of observation and imagery shapes MOMI-related brain network organization, with implications for optimizing motor training protocols and EEG-based assessments of motor simulation states.

papers.title: Lateralized amyloid PET uptake and beta-band connectivity in relation to cognition in temporal lobe epilepsy.
papers.abstract: We examined focus-relative amyloid PET asymmetry and its associations with resting-state EEG connectivity and processing speed in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE). Thirty adults with clinically assigned MTLE (19 right-focus, 11 left-focus) underwent 18F-florapronol PET and resting-state EEG. Regional standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs) and sensor-level weighted phase lag index (wPLI) were evaluated using paired comparisons, rank correlations and exploratory bootstrap indirect-association models. Cognitive data were available for 26 participants, including Digit Symbol Coding (DSC) for 25. Under the original analytical convention, mean medial temporal SUVR was 1.066 ipsilaterally and 1.013 contralaterally (difference 0.053, 95% CI [0.013, 0.093]; p = 0.011; Cohen's dz = 0.500). The contrast differed by focus side (interaction p = 0.002) and was 0.038 under source-table reconstruction (p = 0.075). Ipsilateral SUVR correlated with inter-hemispheric beta wPLI (ρ = 0.617, q = 0.034 across 240 tests). The intra-contralateral association (ρ = 0.536) did not survive this broader correction. Indirect estimates for Trail Making Test A (0.279, 95% bootstrap CI [0.043, 0.761]) and DSC (0.151, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.114, 0.476]) did not survive correction across 136 models. Regional medial temporal PET uptake was associated with beta-band scalp connectivity in this small cohort, while focus-side heterogeneity and labeling sensitivity limit a uniform ipsilateral interpretation. Processing-speed indirect associations were exploratory and did not establish compensation or causality. Replication with structural correction, longer EEG sampling and longitudinal cognitive follow-up is required.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Cardiac Electrophysiology Ethics, Explainability, Equity, and the Road Ahead.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming cardiac electrophysiology (EP) by enabling automated interpretation of electrocardiograms, intracardiac electrograms, wearable sensor data, and imaging modalities. These technologies promise improved diagnostic accuracy, procedural efficiency, and personalized risk stratification across a wide spectrum of arrhythmia care. However, the integration of AI into clinical EP raises important ethical, practical, and regulatory concerns. Many current models function as opaque systems with limited explainability, while training datasets often lack adequate representation across sex, race, geography, and socioeconomic status. These limitations raise the risk of biased performance, reduced generalizability, and erosion of clinician trust. Furthermore, cost, infrastructure requirements, and regulatory complexity threaten equitable global adoption. This review examines the ethical foundations of AI in electrophysiology, focusing on dataset bias, fairness, explainability, and accountability. We discuss the clinical consequences of black box models, outline strategies to improve transparency, and explore emerging regulatory and legal frameworks. Finally, we highlight future horizons including digital twins, multimodal risk engines, and real time procedural guidance systems. Responsible deployment of AI in EP will require rigorous validation, continuous monitoring, clinician oversight, and intentional efforts to ensure equitable access across diverse populations.

papers.title: A Rounding Error Dressed as Reform: The Implications of a Large Private Health Insurance Company's Prior Authorization Concession for the Electrophysiology Patient.
Long-lasting survival, migration and functional maturation of transplanted human reprogrammed neurons in vivo.
papers.abstract: Direct reprogramming of glial progenitor cells (GPCs) into induced neurons (iNs) represents a promising strategy for future brain regenerative therapies. This approach uses forced expression of neuronal fate-determining genes to convert non-neuronal cells into neurons, bypassing a pluripotent intermediate stage and enabling potential in vivo applications. However, evidence for long-term survival and maturation of human reprogrammed neurons in vivo remains limited. Here, we present a longitudinal in vivo analysis of human iNs following transplantation into the immunodeficient mouse cortex. Using 3D cultures of reprogrammed human iNs to enhance graft survival, we demonstrate survival of human iNs for up to 5 months post-transplantation with a proportion of cells remaining up to 10 months. The transplanted cells exhibit widespread migration from the grafted core into anatomically connected brain regions and protracted neuronal maturation, reflected by increased cellular complexity and expression of neuronal markers. Functional analyses reveal gradual electrophysiological maturation and the establishment of afferent synaptic connectivity with host circuits. Importantly, non-reprogrammed GPC grafts retain their glial identity. Together, these findings provide in vivo evidence for long-term survival, neuronal maturation and long-range migration in the intact mouse brain, supporting their potential for future cell repair strategies.

papers.title: Consensus on components of psychological treatment for depression to reduce symptoms and target relapse risk factors in young adults: A modified Delphi study.
papers.abstract: Depression is increasingly prevalent in young adults and relapse is common. This study aimed to obtain consensus on Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT)-based treatment components considered important by experts for reducing symptoms and targeting relapse risk factors in young adults (18-25 years). We conducted a modified-Delphi study of three survey rounds, two panels and a consensus meeting. Academics/clinicians (n = 46) and young adult experts-by-experience (n = 24) rated treatment components, therapist competencies, relapse risk factors and interventions, content of relapse-prevention sessions, and post-treatment relapse-prevention strategies. Items were rated on 1-9 Likert scales. "Consensus-important" was defined as ≥70% of either panel rating the item 7-9 and ≤15% rating 1-3. Behavioural experiments were the highest-rated CBT component in both panels, though the target differed. The Academic/Clinician panel rated experiments targeting negative automatic thoughts highest (97%, n = 30) while the Young Adult panel rated those targeting rumination highest (71%, n = 24). Social isolation/loneliness, stress in relationships and cognitive biases were the top-rated relapse risk factors pooled across both panels. Identifying and challenging negative automatic thoughts, problem solving and behavioural activation often reached consensus as important to target relapse risk factors. Consensus was reached on the content of relapse prevention session(s) with identifying triggers rated most highly by both panels. The findings identify stakeholder-endorsed candidate treatment components for co-design and prospective evaluation of feasibility, effectiveness and relapse risk reduction. A modular approach may be beneficial, including core CBT components and modules targeting relapse risk factors such as social isolation/loneliness, interpersonal stress, cognitive biases, sleep and rumination. Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/gu7tm; DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/GU7TM).

papers.title: Sleep quality and its associated factors among community-dwelling patients with severe mental disorders in Minhang District, Shanghai: A cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common in severe mental disorders (SMD), but community-based epidemiological data in China are scarce. This study examined the prevalence and correlates of poor sleep quality and tested the indirect pathways of psychological distress in the association between social support and sleep. Using 2022 baseline data from a community survey in Shanghai, we included 3797 SMD patients (mean age 54.9 years; 51.6% female; 64.1% schizophrenia-spectrum). Sleep quality was assessed with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI; poor defined as >5), social support with PSSS, anxiety with GAD-7, and depression with PHQ-9. Hierarchical multivariable regression, bootstrap mediation (5000 resamples), and K-means clustering were applied. Mean PSQI was 5.14, and 39.3% had poor sleep. The full model explained 27.8% of variance. PHQ-9 was the strongest independent correlate of poor sleep. Comorbidity (OR = 1.48, 95% CI 1.23-1.77) and lower household income increased risk, whereas no hospitalization history was associated with lower odds of poor sleep. The indirect effect via depression accounted for 81.4% of the total association between social support and sleep, while that via anxiety accounted for 57.8%; the PSSS×PHQ-9 interaction was significant. Three sleep phenotypes were identified: mild (36.1%, mean PSQI 2.7), moderate (43.4%, mean 4.8), and severe (20.5%, mean 10.2), with PHQ-9 as the strongest discriminator. Poor sleep is highly prevalent in community SMD patients. Depression appears central in the indirect pathway from social support to sleep. Integrating depression management, social support enhancement, and phenotype-based stratification warrants further investigation to improve sleep.

papers.title: Tau phosphorylation from neuronal adaptation to Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Tau phosphorylation is classically associated with neurodegeneration, yet similar phosphorylation patterns emerge during physiological states and acute stress responses. How these overlapping patterns of phosphorylated Tau (pTau) relate to neuronal adaptation and Alzheimer's disease pathology remains unresolved. We synthesize findings from human to rodent and fly brains and from neuronal cell models, across neurodevelopment, sleep, hibernation, cellular stress, and disease. Across these contexts, pTau changes are associated with altered Tau localization and functions involving synaptic transmission, mitochondrial activity, RNA metabolism, and genomic integrity. Physiological and acute stress responses are generally transient and reversible, whereas aging, repeated stress, and amyloid-β-associated stress can promote persistent pTau accumulation, impaired clearance, aggregation, and neurodegeneration. We propose that pathological Tau phosphorylation reflects dysregulation of a shared adaptive response rather than activation of an entirely distinct pathway. The critical determinants may be phosphorylation persistence, subcellular localization, proteoform composition, and the capacity to restore Tau homeostasis.

papers.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea and Alzheimer's disease pathology: a review of plausible pathological mechanisms and potential modifying impact of hypertension.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is estimated to account for up to 75% of all dementia cases, of which there is a global prevalence of 50 million. There are no curative treatments available for AD dementia, therefore, early identification of risk factors is paramount. Up to 40% of all dementia cases may be attributable to modifiable risk factors. One such risk factor is poor sleep. Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is a common sleep disorder characterised by repeated upper airway collapse, contributing to intermittent hypoxaemia and sleep fragmentation. Hypertension is frequently comorbid with OSA and is an established risk factor for dementia, with recent literature exploring potential mechanistic contributions to AD pathogenesis. Despite current literature exploring associations between OSA and hypertension on AD individually, little research has investigated the potential combined impact of these two pervasive disorders. To this end, this review will synthesise existing literature investigating potential pathogenic mechanisms between OSA and AD, including oxidative stress and altered sleep architecture. Further, shared pathophysiological consequences of OSA and hypertension will be reviewed in the context of AD to highlight the potential for effective management in mid-life to preserve neurological and cognitive health in late life.

papers.title: Abnormal sleep duration and sarcopenia are jointly associated with adverse depressive trajectories in adults aged ≥45: Evidence from a longitudinal cohort study.
papers.abstract: Abnormal sleep duration (ASD) and sarcopenia are highly prevalent. However, their combined effects on dynamic depressive trajectories remain unclear. This study aimed to explore the associations of coexisting ASD and sarcopenia with first-onset depressive symptoms and depressive symptom trajectories in adults aged ≥45 years. Data were derived from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. A total of 11,295 and 6739 participants were included in cross-sectional, cohort studies and trajectory analysis. Sarcopenia was diagnosed based on the AWGS 2025 criteria, and ASD was defined as sleep duration <6 h or >8 h. Depressive symptoms were assessed using the CES-d-10 scale. Latent class growth model was used to identify depressive trajectories, and multinomial logistic regression was applied to analyze the relationship. ASD combined with sarcopenia was associated with an increased hazard of depressive symptoms based on cross-sectional and cohort study. Three distinct depressive trajectories were identified: persistently low-level normal trajectory (Cluster 1), slowly elevating depressive trajectory (Cluster 2), rapidly elevating depressive trajectory (Cluster 3). After adjusting for covariates (age, gender, education, marital status, smoking, chronic diseases, etc.), ASD combined with sarcopenia group had a significantly higher odds of belonging to cluster 3 (OR=4.130, 95%CI: 2.455-6.948) and cluster 2 (OR=2.436, 95%CI: 1.700-3.941) compared to the reference trajectory. ASD and sarcopenia are jointly associated with first-onset depressive symptoms and adverse depressive trajectories in adults aged ≥45, with a stronger link to rapidly elevating trajectories, which emphasizes the value of integrated psychosomatic screening and intervention targeting ASD and sarcopenia for the management of depressive symptom progression.

papers.title: Somatic burden versus silent toxicity: Distinct longitudinal pathways linking gastric and hepatic diseases to depression.
papers.abstract: We still don't know much about how diseases of specific digestive organs might lead to depression. We hypothesized that gastric and hepatic diseases contribute to depression through distinct longitudinal pathways due to their biological differences. We analyzed five waves (2011-2020) of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), including 24,065 adults aged ≥ 45 years. Participants were classified into control, stomach disease, liver disease, and comorbid groups. We used linear mixed-effects models to examine longitudinal associations with depressive symptoms (CES-D) and causal mediation analyses to assess the roles of physical pain, sleep duration, and systemic inflammation (C-reactive protein). Over the 9-year follow-up, both stomach disease (β = 2.27, 95% CI: 1.94-2.59) and liver disease (β = 1.39, 95% CI: 0.45-2.32) were associated with higher depressive symptoms. For stomach disease, physical pain and sleep disturbance jointly mediated > 50% of the association. In contrast, these somatic factors did not mediate the liver-depression link. C-reactive protein showed no clinically meaningful mediation for either condition. Gastric and hepatic diseases showed differential longitudinal associations with depressive symptoms. Stomach disease-associated depression was largely attenuated by somatic burden, whereas the liver-depression association persisted after accounting for measured physical pain and sleep disturbance. These findings suggest potentially distinct pathways, though causality cannot be established and the association was not explained by measured pain and sleep duration in this study; unmeasured somatic symptoms may still contribute. Clinicians should consider proactive depression screening in patients with liver disease even when physical symptoms appear mild.

papers.title: Clinical and biomarker predictors of α-synuclein seeding in cognitive impairment and motor parkinsonism.
papers.abstract: Dopamine transporter (DAT) imaging and α-synuclein seed amplification assay (SAA) are biomarkers for Lewy body disease (LBD). We aimed to identify clinical and biomarker factors associated with SAA positivity in patients with cognitive impairment and frequent motor parkinsonism. Dual-phase DAT positron emission tomography (PET) scans, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) phosphorylated-tau/β-amyloid ratio (PTAR) measurement, and SAA were performed in 108 patients, including 99 with motor parkinsonism. Diagnoses, which were not mutually exclusive, included normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH, N = 60), Alzheimer's disease (AD, N = 53), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB, N = 43), vascular cognitive impairment (VCI, N = 23), progressive supranuclear palsy (N = 3), and semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (N = 1). We investigated clinical and biomarker factors associated with SAA positivity, including clinical diagnoses, clinical features, striatal DAT uptake, and log-transformed PTAR (LN-PTAR), and examined whether SAA positivity was associated with dopaminergic degeneration and regional perfusion measured by dual-phase DAT PET. SAA was positive in 50 patients (46.3%), including 30 of 43 (69.8%) with DLB and 47 of 99 (47.5%) with motor parkinsonism. Seven (14.0%) SAA-positive patients showed normal DAT uptake. Among clinical diagnoses, DLB and AD were associated with a higher likelihood of SAA positivity, whereas NPH and VCI were associated with a lower likelihood. Among clinical features, cognitive fluctuations and rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder were independently associated with SAA positivity. Among biomarker measures, lower posterior putamen DAT uptake and a higher LN-PTAR were independently associated with SAA positivity. SAA positivity was associated with lower posterior putamen DAT uptake on delayed-phase DAT PET but not with perfusion changes on early-phase DAT PET. These findings suggest that SAA provides complementary information to clinical diagnosis and DAT imaging for evaluating possible LBD, particularly in patients with biomarker evidence of coexisting AD pathology.

papers.title: The views on infant sleep questionnaire: A confirmatory factor analysis in an Australian context.
papers.abstract: Parental beliefs about infant sleep shape caregiving practices, infant development, and parental wellbeing. The Views oN Infant Sleep (VNIS) questionnaire was designed to assess these beliefs across three domains: Closeness, Independence, and Night-Waking. This study aimed to validate the questionnaire for the first time in an Australian context, in a sample of 111 pregnant women. Women completed an anonymous online questionnaire containing the 12-item VNIS. Confirmatory factor analysis was conducted in MPlus, using a weighted least squares estimator to evaluate the proposed three-factor structure. Findings provided partial support for the three-factor model. Incremental and residual fit indices were strong (comparative fit index = 0.97; Tucker-Lewis index = 0.96; weighted root mean square residual = 0.76) and the chi-square to degrees-of-freedom ratio indicated acceptable fit (1.75). Global fit was borderline (root mean square error of approximation = 0.08, 90% confidence interval = 0.05-0.11). All items loaded significantly onto their intended factors, however item performance varied. Independence items showed consistently strong loadings, while Closeness items ranged from moderate to strong with one weaker indicator. Night-Waking items were more variable, including one item below acceptable thresholds. Inter-factor correlations were strong (r = 0.58-0.71), indicating substantial coherence and limited distinctiveness between components. The VNIS questionnaire captures multidimensional parental beliefs about infant sleep but requires refinement to strengthen reliability and discriminant validity. Further cross-cultural and longitudinal research is needed to support its broader applicability in diverse clinical and research contexts including to fathers and non-birthing partners.

papers.title: LIBPhys-EGG: An open-access multichannel electrogastrography and accelerometry dataset for reproducible research in gastrointestinal electrophysiology.
papers.abstract: Surface electrogastrography records gastrointestinal myoelectric activity non-invasively from the abdominal surface. Despite decades of investigation, clinical adoption remains limited by low signal-to-noise ratio, motion artifacts, and the lack of standardized public datasets. This work presents a multichannel electrogastrography dataset acquired using a wearable sensor belt, synchronized with tri-axial accelerometry, designed to support reproducible research in gastrointestinal signal processing and machine learning. The dataset (LIBPhys-EGG) includes 30 recording sessions from 15 healthy adults, totaling 111.8 h of multichannel physiological data. Primary session duration averaged 5.16 ± 1.22 h, covering fasting, meal ingestion, and post-prandial periods. Four bipolar electrogastrography channels and a tri-axial accelerometer were sampled at 1000 Hz. We release raw data with synchronized annotations, a recommended pipeline, feature selection methodology, and a benchmark classification task distinguishing pre- versus post-prandial states. LIBPhys-EGG captured strong physiological changes post-meal. Features measuring signal power and amplitude variability increased substantially across 13 high-quality recordings from 7 unique participants, with large effect sizes (Cohen's dz up to 2.06, p<0.002). Random Forest achieved 0.93 accuracy and 0.966 AUC-ROC using 14 features on recording-level split data; for the same model, leave-one-subject-out validation yielded 0.690 ± 0.198 accuracy. This open dataset offers high-resolution, multichannel sEGG with synchronized motion signals and event annotations, enabling development and benchmarking of noise-robust signal processing and machine-learning methods. It also facilitates analysis of spatial signal distribution and electrode placement. We anticipate this resource will accelerate non-invasive GI research and contribute to standardized protocols for future studies.
